periods.analysis: We are opening this run from a position of strength: the General Fund Reserve % is 19.1%, which is 3.1 percentage points above the >=16% policy target. Because this is the first quarter in the arc, I am treating 19.1% as our operating baseline for the structurally balanced budget objective. Finance closed the quarter on time using the OpenGov Budget Book refresh and the Tyler Munis monthly close checklist, with clean feeds from payroll, permits, and the tourism-related sales tax accounts. The result supports Harborview’s AA bond-rating story: growing city, disciplined budget, no drama in the close.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green result by keeping the monthly variance review with department budget liaisons on the first Wednesday after close. Extend the reserve dashboard to show one-year reserve sensitivity for permit revenue and coastal-season sales tax, so Council sees both the strength and the watch-items before Q4. Please have departments certify encumbrances by October 10 so year-end projections stay clean and comparable.

periods.analysis: The General Fund Reserve % finished at 18.8%, down 0.3 percentage points from 19.1% in 2024-Q3, and still comfortably above the >=16% target. The quarter included normal year-end draws for the winter storm readiness purchase orders, police fleet lease true-up, and final library HVAC retainage, so the small step-down is expected rather than concerning. Finance and department liaisons kept the close orderly; the only notable cleanup item was reclassing three marina maintenance invoices from operating supplies to contracted services before the December book lock. We remain green, and the narrative for Council is simple: Harborview used reserves as planned while preserving a healthy margin.
periods.recommendations: Sustain performance by documenting the Q4 reserve bridge in the Council packet, including the 0.3 percentage-point movement from 2024-Q3 to 2024-Q4. Extend the close checklist to require departments with capital-adjacent operating invoices, especially Public Works and Parks, to flag coding questions five business days before cutoff. Keep the reserve floor stress test in the January budget workshop so we maintain confidence without sounding casual about year-end spending.

periods.analysis: The General Fund Reserve % rose to 19.3%, up 0.5 percentage points from 18.8% in 2024-Q4, and remains green against the >=16% target. The rebound reflects stronger-than-budgeted transient occupancy tax from the winter conference season, slower hiring in two non-sworn cohorts, and timely reimbursement postings for the Seabreeze Avenue drainage grant. I appreciate the departments here: HR, Police, and Public Works all submitted vacancy and overtime updates by the reporting deadline, which made the reserve calculation cleaner. This quarter strengthens the chronological story that Q4 was a planned dip, not a trend break.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green result by continuing the vacancy-rate pulse check with HR before each forecast upload, especially for sworn, inspection, and maintenance classifications. Extend the revenue monitoring tab to separate one-time winter event revenue from recurring sales tax, so we do not accidentally build ongoing commitments on seasonal lift. For Council, frame the 19.3% result as disciplined recovery from 18.8%, with the same >=16% guardrail front and center.

periods.analysis: The General Fund Reserve % increased again to 19.8%, up 0.5 percentage points from 19.3% in 2025-Q1 and 3.8 percentage points above the >=16% target. This is a strong midyear result, helped by development services permit volume on the Harborline Apartments, Baypoint Medical Office, and North Pier mixed-use projects, plus conservative departmental spending through the spring. Finance completed the midyear forecast lock two days early, and departments used the shared ClearPoint comment fields consistently enough that we did not need the usual second-round cleanup. The green status is well earned, and it gives us room to manage growth pressures without weakening the structural balance message.
periods.recommendations: Sustain momentum by converting the midyear forecast process into the template for FY2026 budget development, including the same department certification dates. Extend the permit-revenue analysis with a cohort view by project type, because Harborline-scale activity is helpful but should not be treated as permanent base revenue. Ask departments to identify one operating efficiency each in the next budget memo so the 19.8% reserve level is paired with visible stewardship.

periods.analysis: The General Fund Reserve % is 19.6%, down 0.2 percentage points from 19.8% in 2025-Q2, while still clearly green against the >=16% target. The slight movement is consistent with planned summer service loads: lifeguard staffing at Harborview Beach, Parks seasonal crews on Route P-4, and traffic control support for the PierFest series. Importantly, the departments stayed inside their approved seasonal plans, and Finance matched the temporary staffing batches to the correct program codes before the quarter closed. The arc remains healthy: after two quarters of improvement, Q3 shows controlled use of resources during Harborview’s busiest public-facing season.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the result by keeping summer-event cost tracking separate through the end of the fiscal year, not rolling it into general Parks or Police overtime too early. Extend the Q3 variance note to include PierFest, beach operations, and Route P-4 cleanup as explicit drivers of the 0.2 percentage-point decline. For the next forecast, have department owners confirm whether any seasonal costs will recur at a higher level in 2026 so the structural view stays honest.

periods.analysis: The General Fund Reserve % ended the quarter at 19.1%, down 0.5 percentage points from 19.6% in 2025-Q3, and still 3.1 percentage points above the >=16% target. This is the second consecutive modest decline, so I am calling it green with a friendly nudge: not a problem, but worth explaining cleanly. The main drivers were planned year-end technology renewals, the final match payment on the Coastal Resilience Planning Grant, and higher utility costs at City facilities during the early winter cold snap. Departments met the reporting calendar, and Procurement’s contract log for the Microsoft, Motorola, and CivicPlus renewals gave Finance enough backup to keep the reserve movement transparent.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the green status by preparing a one-page reserve bridge for Council that shows the move from 19.6% to 19.1% and distinguishes planned one-time costs from operating trend. Extend the vendor-renewal calendar into the budget system so major Q4 technology renewals are forecast earlier in the year. Before Q1 close, ask Facilities to flag any utility-rate assumptions that need updating so we do not carry stale winter cost estimates.

periods.analysis: The General Fund Reserve % improved to 19.3%, up 0.2 percentage points from 19.1% in 2025-Q4, and remains green against the >=16% target. That small rebound is exactly what we wanted to see after the Q4 watch-item: revenues posted on schedule, utility pressure eased, and departments held discretionary spending until the revised forecast was loaded. Finance also completed the quarterly reconciliation of grant reimbursements, including the West Harbor Trail invoice set WH-17 through WH-22, which reduced timing noise in the reserve calculation. The broader arc is steady and credible: Harborview is growing quickly, but the budget discipline is keeping pace with the growth.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the improvement by keeping the discretionary-spend review in place through Q2, with exceptions approved only for service-critical needs or Council-directed work. Extend the grant reimbursement tracker to show aging by department, because faster reimbursement posting protects the reserve metric and makes teams look good in the scorecard. Use the Q1 Council update to note the 0.2 percentage-point recovery without over-celebrating; the value is consistency.

periods.analysis: The General Fund Reserve % reached 20.1%, up 0.8 percentage points from 19.3% in 2026-Q1 and 4.1 percentage points above the >=16% target. This is the strongest point in the eight-quarter arc, supported by timely property tax settlement receipts, solid spring retail activity along Marina Boulevard, and continued discipline on departmental operating carryforwards. The Finance team closed the quarter on schedule, and the new budget liaison huddle helped reconcile Fire overtime, Development Services permit revenue, and Parks contract mowing invoices before the ClearPoint update deadline. For a fast-growing AA-rated coastal suburb, this is the kind of green result that lets us be both ambitious and careful.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the 20.1% position by codifying the quarterly budget liaison huddle as a standing process with named backups for every department. Extend the reserve policy discussion in the next Council workshop to include a growth-risk reserve scenario for infrastructure, staffing, and coastal storm volatility while keeping the >=16% floor intact. Use the current strength to pre-fund one-time planning and asset-condition work where appropriate, rather than adding recurring commitments that could soften the structural balance later.

periods.analysis: General Fund reserves remain above target at 18.3%, despite a decline from 18.6%. Proposed FY27 federal funding changes and mitigation opportunities are planning considerations, not Harborview awards.
periods.recommendations: Show approved funding separately from applications and assumptions; preserve the reserve floor when considering capital options.
